preamble: Lowering of the close front vowel /i/ to close-mid /e/. In Old Irish, short i (and u) were lowered to e (and o) when the next syllable had, or once had, the low vowel a or o; the final vowels were later lost, so the lowering is now visible mainly in alternations such as fer 'man' (Proto-Celtic *wiros) against genitive fir (*wirī). In Moroccan Arabic the change is allophonic: the full vowels /a i u/ are realized as [ɑ e o] near an emphatic consonant or q, χ, ʁ, r, with no full vowel in between, and as [æ i u] elsewhere; emphasis spreads most reliably from a consonant to the vowel that directly follows it and towards the beginning of the word.
